common_name: Ladies in Waiting Pitcher Plant (Maroon-Hooded Speckled Sarracenia Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss, never fertilized potting soil, and stand the pot in a tray of rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water at all times; keep total dissolved minerals low, since this hybrid is sensitive to hard tap water.

directions: Bred by botanist Larry Mellichamp at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte from a cross of Sarracenia leucophylla with (S. rubra x S. psittacina), Ladies in Waiting arose from a single seedling given to the North Carolina Botanical Garden in 1985 and was registered as a cultivar with the International Carnivorous Plant Society in 1998. Its stiffly upright pitchers reach about 14 inches, green at the base shading to rich maroon-red toward the top, with dark red veins and white speckling across a ruffled, ridged hood that reflects its leucophylla heritage, while a hairy interior and heavier speckling reveal the psittacina and rubra parentage. Grow in a nutrient-poor, acidic medium of pure sphagnum moss or a 1:1 peat-perlite mix kept permanently wet with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water only, since it is especially sensitive to dissolved minerals and fertilizer. As with other Sarracenia it lures insects to nectar at the pitcher rim, where they slip down the waxy interior walls and are digested to supply nutrients the poor bog soil lacks. Give it full sun for the strongest coloring and allow a natural winter dormancy with reduced water and shorter days.
sources: International Carnivorous Plant Society cultivar registry

common_name: Doreen's Colossus Pitcher Plant (Giant Yellow-Green Sarracenia Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes into a wide, deep container of pure sphagnum moss or a 1:1 peat-perlite mix and stand it in a tray of rain or distilled water at all times; this hybrid's exceptional height calls for a taller pot than most Sarracenia to support its pitchers without tipping.

directions: Traced to a batch of Sarracenia flava x oreophila seedlings that circulated among Pacific Northwest growers in the mid-1990s, Doreen's Colossus was named in honor of British carnivorous plant enthusiast Doreen Smith and is grown for producing some of the tallest pitchers of any Sarracenia hybrid, regularly reaching three feet. Pitchers are vivid yellow-green with bold red veining and a flared, ruffled peristome atop an upright, trumpet-shaped tube, with tall yellow flowers typical of its flava parentage opening in spring before the season's pitchers fully unfurl. Grow in a nutrient-poor, acidic medium of pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite mix kept permanently wet with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water, since fertilizer and mineral-laden tap water damage the roots. As with other pitcher plants it lures insects to nectar at the rim, where they slip down the waxy inner walls and are digested to supply nutrients the poor bog soil lacks. Give it full sun for the strongest color and tallest pitchers, and allow a natural winter dormancy with reduced water and shorter days.

common_name: Appalachian Spring Pitcher Plant (Peach-Flowered Oreophila-Jonesii Sarracenia Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss and stand the pot in a tray of rain or distilled water at all times; because both parent species come from cooler mountain seeps, this hybrid appreciates a shadier, cooler bog site than lowland Sarracenia.

directions: Bred in the 1990s from a cross of two rare mountain endemics, the federally endangered Sarracenia oreophila and Sarracenia rubra subsp. jonesii, Appalachian Spring was selected as three superior clones chosen for vigorous growth and showy peach-to-reddish-orange-to-yellow flowers. Pitchers and blooms lean toward the jonesii parent in form, greenish-yellow maturing to yellowish-orange with red veining, and the plant produces a strong flush of pitchers in spring and early summer that slows and darkens by midsummer before a second flush appears as weather cools in fall. Grow in a nutrient-poor, acidic medium of pure sphagnum moss or a peat-sand mix kept permanently wet with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water. As with other Sarracenia it lures insects to nectar at the pitcher rim. Because both parent species come from cooler, higher-elevation seeps, give this hybrid a slightly shadier and cooler bog site than Gulf Coast Sarracenia prefer.

common_name: Read's Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia x Readii, Natural Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes into pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite mix, never fertilized potting soil, and keep the pot standing in a tray of rain or distilled water at all times; this naturally occurring cross is also sold under the older synonym Sarracenia x farnhamii.

directions: Grow in a nutrient-poor, acidic medium of pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite mix kept permanently wet with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water. Sarracenia x readii is a naturally occurring hybrid between the white-topped pitcher plant (S. leucophylla) and sweet pitcher plant (S. rubra, most often the Alabama canebrake subspecies alabamensis), found where the ranges of the two parents overlap in the wild and also traded under the older synonym S. x farnhamii. Pitchers are intermediate between the parents, more slender and upright than typical leucophylla but carrying the same white-veined hood coloring over a rubra-like narrow tube. As with other Sarracenia it lures insects to nectar at the pitcher rim, where they slip down the waxy inner walls and are digested to supply nutrients the poor bog soil lacks. Give it full sun for the strongest pitcher color and production, and allow a natural winter dormancy with reduced water and shorter days.

common_name: Swan's Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia x Swaniana, Natural Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes into pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite mix, never fertilized potting soil, and keep the pot standing in a tray of rain or distilled water at all times; this rarely offered natural hybrid was first described from a population near Shallotte, North Carolina.

directions: Grow in a nutrient-poor, acidic medium of pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite mix kept permanently wet with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water. Sarracenia x swaniana is an uncommon naturally occurring hybrid between the purple pitcher plant (S. purpurea) and the hooded pitcher plant (S. minor), first collected near Shallotte, North Carolina, where the ranges of the two low-growing parent species overlap. It combines the squat, water-holding pitcher shape of purpurea with a domed hood recalling minor's helmet-like lid, in a compact, ground-hugging clump. As with other Sarracenia it lures insects to nectar at the pitcher rim, where they slip down the waxy inner walls or become disoriented by translucent hood windows and are digested to supply nutrients the poor bog soil lacks. Give it full sun to light shade for the strongest pitcher color, and allow a natural winter dormancy with reduced water.

common_name: Redbug Pitcher Plant (Dwarf Crimson Sarracenia Rubra Hybrid, US Plant Patent)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss and stand the pot in a tray of rain or distilled water at all times; Redbug is protected by US Plant Patent, so propagate only from nursery-authorized divisions.

directions: Originating as a single seedling at the North Carolina Botanical Garden in the late 1980s from a cross of Sarracenia rubra subsp. rubra (coastal North Carolina) and S. rubra subsp. wherryi (southeastern Alabama), Redbug is a compact, dwarf cultivar protected by US Plant Patent. Its narrow, finely fuzzy pitchers mature from green to a dark crimson red, widening gradually above the middle before narrowing at the mouth, and are topped by a hood notably larger than either parent species with a distinctive slender filament at its tip. The clump-forming plant produces multiple flushes of pitchers through summer and holds attractive color and texture into winter dormancy. Grow in a nutrient-poor, acidic medium of pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite mix kept permanently wet with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water. Give it full sun for the deepest crimson color, and allow a natural winter dormancy with reduced water.
